Translation industry trends: human-AI collaboration in 2026 and beyond

February 13, 2023
Human translation | Machine Translation | Translation tools

Translation industry trends in 2026

The question is no longer whether AI will replace human translators.

It is how the two work together, and which jobs each does best.

Machine translation has become part of everyday translation work, while the need for human expertise has become more focused, not smaller.

This page covers the translation industry trends that matter to UK businesses in 2026, and what they mean for the way you buy translation.

How big is the translation industry in 2026?

Nimdzi, a research firm that tracks the language industry, estimates that language services reached about USD 72.6 billion in 2025 and will grow to USD 73.4 billion in 2026.

That is much slower growth than its previous edition predicted, which had put 2025 at USD 75.7 billion.

Nimdzi also reports that the industry is highly fragmented, with the top 100 providers making up under a fifth of total industry size.

For buyers, this means a crowded market in which quality, specialism and process matter more than size.

AI translation: from novelty to standard tool

Tools such as Google Translate, DeepL and Microsoft Translator now sit alongside large language models in many translation workflows.

Four developments explain the leap in fluency.

  • Neural machine translation: models that read whole sentences in context, so the output sounds far more natural than earlier statistical systems.
  • Large language models: systems that handle tone, register and instructions, so you can ask for formal or informal output.
  • Adaptive machine translation: engines that learn from translator corrections and client feedback.
  • Multimodal AI: tools that work on text, audio and images, such as automatic subtitle drafts and text inside photographs.

These tools are fast and consistent, and they suit high volumes of low-risk content such as internal notes or product catalogues.

Why human translators still matter

AI handles speed and volume, but professional translators provide what a machine cannot guarantee.

  • Cultural intelligence: understanding idioms, humour and references that do not translate literally. A piece of British understatement rarely lands the same way in Brazilian Portuguese.
  • Transcreation: rewriting marketing copy, slogans and brand messaging so they work emotionally in the target market.
  • Accountability: a named professional stands behind the result, which matters for medical, legal and financial content.
  • Strategic alignment: keeping translations consistent with your tone of voice, terminology and brand positioning.

Accountability is also a legal point in the UK.

GOV.UK states that a certified translation must carry the translator's written confirmation that it is a true and accurate translation of the original document, plus the date, their full name and their contact details.

A machine cannot give that confirmation, so official documents submitted to UK authorities still need a human translator.

Key translation trends to watch

Augmented translation workflows

Translation management systems and computer-assisted translation tools now use AI to suggest terminology, pull matches from translation memory and automate formatting.

That frees linguists to spend their time on judgement rather than repetition.

Specialisation over generalisation

As AI covers general content, human translators concentrate on specialist fields.

Examples include legal translation for contracts and litigation, medical translation for clinical documentation, financial translation for regulatory reporting, and creative localisation for games, film and advertising.

Audiovisual and real-time localisation

Streaming, live events and online video keep pushing demand for subtitling, dubbing and voice-over.

AI now drafts transcripts and first-pass subtitles, and human linguists check timing, tone and accuracy before release.

Quality standards and AI governance

Organisations are setting rules for how AI translation may be used.

Two international standards are the reference points: ISO 17100 sets requirements for translation services, and ISO 18587 sets requirements for the human post-editing of machine translation output.

Ask any provider which standard their process follows, and who reviews machine output before it reaches you.

The modern translation workflow

The most effective processes combine machine speed with human review.

  1. Machine translation first pass: a neural engine produces a draft quickly.
  2. Human post-editing: a translator corrects meaning, fluency and cultural fit.
  3. Subject matter review: a specialist in law, medicine, finance or technology checks terminology.
  4. Quality assurance: automated checks and human proofreading catch what remains.
  5. Feedback loop: corrections go back into translation memory so the next project starts from a better base.

Not every project needs every step.

A website translation project may combine machine drafts with transcreation of key pages, while a contract will go straight to a specialist legal translator.

What this means for your business

Match the method to the risk.

Use machine translation for content that only needs to be understood, and use professional human translation for anything that is published, signed, submitted to an authority or tied to your brand.

BeTranslated blends technology with human specialists, and every project is quoted per project, based on your languages, content and purpose.

To discuss the right approach for your content, request a quote.

Frequently asked questions

Will AI replace human translators?

Not for work where accuracy, accountability or tone matter. AI handles volume and speed, while human translators handle judgement, culture and responsibility for the final text.

How big is the global translation industry?

Nimdzi estimates language services at about USD 72.6 billion in 2025, rising to USD 73.4 billion in 2026. Other research firms use different methods, so figures vary between reports.

What is machine translation post-editing?

It is the process in which a human linguist reviews and corrects machine-translated text. ISO 18587 sets requirements for full human post-editing and for the competence of post-editors.

Do UK authorities accept AI translations?

For official purposes they expect a certified translation. GOV.UK says it must include the translator's confirmation that it is a true and accurate translation, the date, their name and their contact details.

How do you choose between machine and human translation?

Consider the risk if the translation is wrong. Machine translation suits internal or low-risk content, and human translation suits legal, medical, financial and public-facing material.
